concepts.def: Lovers' first meeting forms a 14-line sonnet together.
Tension between destiny and characters' choices.
Male reputation drives Tybalt's duel and Capulet's rage.
Love is light; the world it must hide in is dark.
Pity and fear purged by the lovers' final sacrifice.
Houses reconcile only over their children's tombs.

walkthroughs.body_html: When Romeo and Juliet first meet in Act 1 Scene 5, their dialogue forms a perfect Petrarchan-Shakespearean sonnet. The form itself argues their love is fated: their voices fit a 14-line frame as if pre-written. The 'holy palmer' imagery elevates lust to pilgrimage.

Is the tragedy fated or chosen? The Prologue insists on fate, yet Romeo's choices - crashing the ball, killing Tybalt, taking the poison without waiting - drive each turn. Shakespeare leaves the tension open, asking how far 'star-crossed' lives are still self-authored.

Lord Capulet's threat to drag Juliet 'on a hurdle' to marry Paris exposes how patriarchal honour treats daughters as property. Tybalt's duels and Mercutio's bawdy jokes both stem from a masculine code in which words like 'biting the thumb' demand blood. Love struggles against this code.
